newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ex-communists conclude reformist congress.
newsitem.headline: German ex-communists conclude reformist congress.

text.p: Germany's ex-communists on Sunday wound up a party congress at which they agreed to cooperate with mainstream opposition parties to oust Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government at the next elections.

Reformers in the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), the successor to the hardline communists ruled who East Germany, hailed the conference as a victory in their drive to lead the party away from its stance as a purely opposition group.
"The PDS has changed on a whole range of issues," said party chairman Lothar Bisky, who was re-elected unopposed to his post with fellow reformers also occupying all the main party jobs.

Delegates approved a range of policy documents and statute changes at the congress in the northeastern city of Schwerin but the most important document was a resolution for the party to make a "direct contribution" to ousting Kohl's coalition.

"The important thing is to make real changes in society and we won't manage those alone," said PDS parliamentary leader Gregor Gysi, whose charisma and telegenic personality have made him the party's highest profile official.
Marxist members had wanted the party to have no truck with a political system which they fundamentally oppose.
But the declaration clears the way for the PDS to work more closely with Germany's two mainstream opposition parties, the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens.
Unfortunately for the PDS, large sections of both the SPD and the Greens are not so keen to work with them.
Their leaders say the PDS has not distanced itself enough from the heritage of the communist SED party which ruled East Germany with an iron fist for decades.
But Gysi said those parties would come to realise they needed help from the PDS, which is particularly strong in eastern Germany, to oust Kohl at elections due next year.
"The only people who decide to exclude us are the people who know cooperation is inevitable," he said.
The resolution leaves open whether the PDS would simply offer tacit support to any future SPD-Green government, as it does in one east German state, or might actively participate.
Members of Kohl's coalition were quick to dismiss the party congress as a cosmetic exercise which would not alter the true nature of the PDS and its Cold War heritage.
"The PDS/SED remains a party of old Stalinists and neo-communists," said Michael Glos, the parliamentary leader of Kohl's Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union.
"Its discussions have made clear once again that the PDS/SED wants another republic from the one described in the Bonn constitution," Glos said.

The PDS attracts between four and six percent support nationally but around 20 percent in the east, where it portrays itself as a champion of those who feel let down by the main parties in the painful change from communism to capitalism.
